Published by
Physics-informed machine learning for wetting hydrodynamics
Article preview
Highlights
Abstract
abstract:
Abstract
This study presents a data-driven approach for modeling wetting hydrodynamics phenomena in the form of droplet transport on chemically heterogeneous surfaces, utilizing prior physical knowledge. The training datasets are generated using direct numerical simulations of the two-phase Stokes equations, applicable in the low Reynolds number limit. The resulting data-driven models are based on the Fourier neural operator and are trained to correct the time derivative of the contact line as predicted by a low-order asymptotic approximation, an approach that was proven to be accurate and generalizable in earlier studies that focused on wetting hydrodynamics in the long-wave regime. More specifically, two data-driven models are trained to augment the low-order contact line velocity prediction: (i) a model focusing on correcting the purely translational velocity component of the droplet, and (ii) a model focusing on the higher-order corrections to the contact line velocity. The corrected contact line velocity is then used to advance the solution in time, using standard time-integration schemes. The resulting physics-informed machine learning workflow is proven to accurately capture the contact line dynamics on a range of different substrate heterogeneity profiles and can provide a reliable and efficient alternative to costly direct numerical simulations in optimization tasks, where a large number of simulations are needed.

  - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
  - generic: Wetting hydrodynamics describes the dynamic interaction of liquids and solid surfaces in the presence of a gas phase, a process that is strongly influenced by the physical properties of each phase. At the heart of this class of phenomena lies the concept of the contact angle, namely the angle formed at the junction where three phases meet (typically solid, liquid and vapor), the so-called contact line. Practically, small contact angles indicate a high degree of wetting, where the liquid spreads easily on the solid surface, while large contact angles signify non-wetting behavior. Surface tension also plays a crucial role in wetting hydrodynamics, as the cohesive force between liquid molecules that tends to minimize the liquid’s surface area. Therefore, when a droplet is deposited on a surface, its spreading behavior is driven by the balance between surface tension, viscous dissipation, and the liquid-solid interactions, while other forces can come into play (e.g. gravity, electric fields, etc.) [1], [2], [3].
  - generic: Understanding wetting hydrodynamics is crucial for various practical applications. In materials science and engineering, it is essential for the design of coatings, adhesives, and surface treatments to control surface wettability [1]. In microfluidics, wetting hydrodynamics governs the behavior of tiny liquid droplets in micro-scale devices (e.g. lab-on-a-chip devices), influencing processes such as mixing, transport, and droplet manipulation [4]. Wetting also affects the behavior of liquids in biological systems, such as the spreading of tears on the eye surface [5] and the transport of water through the plants’ xylem [6]. Nonetheless, the inherently multi-scale nature of the wetting phenomenon [2] introduces such complexities (e.g. contact line hysteresis and stick-slip behavior due to nanoscale surface defects) that innovations in relevant applications are mainly driven by experiments.
  - generic: To allow for a moving contact line, a small length scale, typically the slip length, is invoked to relax the classical hydrodynamic description in the vicinity of the contact line and mitigate the stress singularities that would have occurred otherwise [1], [2]. In this context, the development of models for moving contact lines at small capillary numbers started from the work of Voinov [7], which was then generalized to arbitrary viscosity ratios by Cox [8]. Since these seminal works, further developments followed depending on the situations under consideration and their associated modeling assumptions [1], [2]. For example, when the contact angles and capillary numbers are small, and the ambient fluid phase is neglected, lubrication theory becomes applicable. In this regime, the governing equations can be treated asymptotically. This approach, as shown by Lacey [9], Hocking [10], and others, leads to evolution equations for the contact line shape and avoids the difficulties associated with numerically resolving the dynamics everywhere. For larger contact angles, analytical work is arguably more limited, but noteworthy contributions in the context of dip coating flows where the contact line is driven by a prescribed speed include those by Snoeijer [11] and Chan et al. [12] who proposed a generalized lubrication equation for the local slope that applies to arbitrary angles, which was recently extended to larger capillary numbers [13].
  - generic: While asymptotic analysis can provide approximate solutions for the contact line velocity in simple wetting scenarios, numerical modeling provides the opportunity to study more complex cases. Several computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methodologies were used to simulate dynamic contact lines, including volume-of-fluid (VOF) [14], [15], level-set [16], [17], and phase-field [18], [19] methods, among many other contributions. In these methods, even when no-slip boundary conditions are applied, slip is implicit due to the thickness of the liquid-gas interface, requiring strong mesh refinement around the contact line. Focusing on the modeling of microscopic features, even though no-slip boundary conditions are typically used on the solid substrate, an effective slip emerges due to the fact that the liquid-gas interface is captured on a finite-sized grid [20]. This effective slip was the subject of further studies by Afkhami and coworkers [15], [21], where Cox’s theory [8] was used to analyze numerical models for mesh independent simulations of dynamic contact line problems.
  - generic: In tandem with reduced-order models and numerical simulations, the present study introduces a data-driven component in the overall workflow for modeling contact line phenomena by invoking the motion of isolated droplets on chemically heterogeneous surfaces as a model system. The advances in graphics processing unit (GPU) hardware and machine learning (ML) frameworks facilitated the adoption of data-driven methods in several branches of fluid mechanics [22]. Topics such as turbulence modeling, coherent structures identification, flow control, and reduced-order modeling have significantly benefited from the progress in ML [23]. More relevant to the present study, data-driven methods were also utilized for the study of multi-phase flow systems. To predict the kinematics of spherical particles [24] and bubbles [25] in turbulent flows, data-driven models were developed to improve traditional, analytically derived models that were otherwise restricted by a limited regime of applicability. In the context of thin film flows, data-driven methods were used to develop both physics-agnostic and physics-informed models to predict the film thickness [26]. Algorithmic improvement via data-driven models were also suggested for the mean curvature estimation of the two-fluid interface in the level-set method [27]. Furthermore, approaches ranging from physics-informed neural network enrichment to multifidelity frameworks have demonstrated significant potential for addressing closure problems in reduced order models of multiscale systems [28], [29]. Even though many studies have been devoted on this topic, the potential of data-driven methods to enhance the study of multi-phase flows remains largely unexplored [30].
  - generic: "The present study builds on two recent works that presented PIML workflows for modeling droplet dynamics. The first study considered the motion of thin droplets on chemically heterogeneous horizontal substrates [31], where the best performing approach was based on evolving a Cox–Voinov-type contact line model derived from Lacey’s work [9], which is augmented with a data-driven component that focuses on correcting the higher harmonics of the contact line velocity. This approach was shown to perform much better in terms of accuracy and out-of-distribution gereralizability, compared to a fully data-driven approach where the neural network is applied autoregressively to predict the future state of the contact line. The second study considered droplet motion on inclined surfaces under the influence of gravity [32]. Cox’s reduced-order model [8] was augmented by a data-driven component to capture the directed transport and large-scale translational droplet motion induced by gravity. Similar to references [24], [25], the reduced-order models used in the aforementioned studies already encode important physical aspects of the problem and provide a good base solution which the ML-based model is tasked to improve. This strategy falls broadly under the umbrella of physics-informed machine learning (PIML), which can incorporate physical knowledge in multiple ways: by encoding physical constraints in the data preprocessing or network architecture, by embedding governing equations into the loss function (as in physics-informed neural networks), by modifying the optimization procedure, or by coupling data-driven models with reduced-order or physics-based models [33], [34]. Here, the data-driven part learns residual or unmodeled dynamics, while the physical model enforces the known structure implied through Cox’s model."
  - text: "The present study aims to extend the PIML approach for wetting hydrodynamics leveraging a large dataset of direct numerical simulation (DNS), considering droplet transport on randomly generated heterogeneous horizontal substrates. This is a much more complex task compared to the earlier studies due to the fact that (i) the droplet simulations solve the full Navier–Stokes equations and are not based on the lubrication approximation as in Demou and Savva [31], and (ii) there is no gravity component that can diminish the effect of the higher-order harmonics of the contact line velocity as in Demou and Savva [32]. The key contribution that extends these works is the use of two separate data-driven models which target specific aspects that remain challenging for Cox’s reduced-order model [8]: the first corrects the large-scale translational motion of the droplet (e.g. due to the presence of chemical gradients on the substrate), while the second provides higher-order corrections of the contact line velocity. Another important feature in the proposed workflow is the integration of the open source software"
  - emphasis: Surface Evolver
  - text: for computing apparent contact angles, distinguishing it from earlier works that used perturbative approximations [31], [32], which pertain to nearly circular contact lines and may be further limited to small contact angles. The integrated PIML solver exhibits a speed-up of several orders of magnitude over DNS, enabling optimization and design applications workflows that were previously would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.
  - generic: The remainder of this study is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the mathematical model and numerical methods used to generate the datasets, perform the reduced-order model calculations, train the data-driven models and fairly compare the predicted results against the reference solutions. Furthermore, Section 3 presents the results of the data-driven workflow, after the documentation of the various modeling choices made. Finally, concluding remarks and a summary of the key findings of this study are offered in Section 4.
